Konstantinidis 8 , Joe Brown ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-5200-4148 4 , PAASIM Trial Consortium , Rassul Nalá 9 na2 & … Karen Levy ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-0968-9401 1 , 3 na2 Show authors Nature Water ( 2026 ) Cite this article Save article View saved research 453 Accesses Metrics details Abstract We conducted a matched-control study to assess the impact of substantial improvements to the urban water system in Beira, Mozambique, on child health and enteric infections. The intervention reduced overall infection with individual pathogens by 10% and co-infection by 13%, especially among children with more than two pathogens. However, we found no impact of the intervention on infection with bacteria or protozoa as classes of pathogens, nor on diarrhoea, child growth or child mortality outcomes. We found no association between direct household water connections—independent of intervention status—on any outcomes. Our evidence points to potential impacts of the intervention on enteric pathogen infections, but estimates were imprecise. The impact of the intervention may have been limited by the lack of provision of continuous, reliable water supply and lack of safe water storage, leading to household contamination and infection from non-water-supply routes of exposure. Bacterial infection Diarrhoea Intestinal diseases Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene Interventions for Child Health Main Access to water is a human right and fundamental to economic development and growth. Provision of safe drinking water is one of the greatest public health achievements of the twentieth century 1 ; however, 2.2 billion people—846 million in urban areas and nearly 50% in sub-Saharan Africa—lack access to a safely managed drinking water source 2 . Poor access to drinking water—alongside lack of access to sanitation and poor hygiene—is responsible for over a million annual deaths due to diarrhoea 3 . Beyond diarrhoea, repeated enteropathogen infections, regardless of symptoms, can lead to linear growth faltering 3 . In Mozambique, 27% of stunting is attributed to unimproved water and sanitation 4 . Improvements to water systems can improve drinking water quality and increase the water available for hygiene and other health behaviours. Movement up the water access ladder—from unimproved to safely managed supply—is estimated to reduce diarrhoea by 37%; however, most studies have focused on improving water quality at the household through either chlorination or filtration 3 . The five studies that have evaluated improvements to water service delivery in urban areas have found mixed impacts on diarrhoea 5 . A matched-controlled study in India found that an intervention that provided households with continuous water supply had no impact on diarrhoea and bloody diarrhoea but did find an impact on typhoid and bloody diarrhoea in low-income children, compared to households that received intermittent supply 6 . A household-matched study in two Yemini villages found a non-statistically significant increase in childhood diarrhoea in households with piped water and sanitation improvements compared to those using traditional well water and water trucks. Given the poor fidelity of the intervention, the authors concluded that no water improvements should be made without first ensuring adequately reliable provision 7 . An intervention in Morocco to promote household-level water connections found no impact on diarrhoea 8 . A double-difference analysis of neighbourhood-level water connections in Argentina, however, found a 47% reduction in diarrhoea risk among children in neighbourhoods who received connections compared to those that did not 9 . Similarly, in Bangladesh, a randomized trial of in-line chlorination systems—with no additional infrastructural improvements—reduced diarrhoeal disease among children under five by 23%, compared to controls
